title: Back then
job: Habits and states in the past; then against now
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A PAST HABIT NEEDS NO NEW TENSE AND THIS MODULE OPENS NONE FOR IT. pūrvam or bālye in front, L1-M4's ordinary participial past at the end, and a frequency word in the middle: pūrvam aham pratidinam vidyālayam gatavān is 'I used to go to school every day'. Every piece of that has been on the ladder since Level 1.

ONE CELL OPENS AND IT IS NAMED FOR WHAT IT IS: āsīt, 'was', and it IS an imperfect. It is the only imperfect this course writes. agacchat, akarot and abhavat are real Sanskrit and are written nowhere here, because a lakāra is a whole paradigm and this module buys one word.

āsīt IS THIRD SINGULAR AND NOTHING ELSE. There is no first person of it here, so aham āsīt is not a sentence. To say 'I was a student' this course still writes aham chātraḥ with no copula at all, exactly as L1-M1 taught, and lets pūrvam carry the pastness.

āsīt EXISTS BECAUSE THE PARTICIPIAL PAST HAS NO FORM FOR A STATE. gatavān says an action was completed; nothing in that family says how a thing STOOD. And asti is present by definition, so a verbless past sentence would simply read as a present one.

ENGLISH 'WAS' COVERS TWO THINGS AND SANSKRIT SPLITS THEM. āsīt is the STATE — how something stood. L2-M8's jātam is the EVENT — that something took place. kim āsīt asks what the situation was; kim jātam asks what happened, and the two are not interchangeable.

ENGLISH MARKS THE HABITUAL PAST IN THE VERB — 'used to', 'would' — AND SANSKRIT DOES NOT MOVE THE VERB AT ALL. The habit lives in pūrvam and pratidinam, and the participle is the same one a single completed action takes. A learner hunting for a special past shape is hunting for something that is not there.

bālye is 'in childhood', the 'in' shape of bālyam — L1-M7's place case doing time instead. The naming shape bālyam is what the thing is called; bālye is when. It points at a stretch of life rather than a date, which is why no calendar is needed.

abhyāsaḥ is 'practice · a regular habit'. It lets a then-and-now sentence NAME the habit instead of only describing it: mama abhyāsaḥ uttamaḥ āsīt says the habit itself was good, which no string of participles can say.

THE PARTICIPIAL PAST FORKS ONCE, AT THE SPEAKER, and a then-and-now paragraph is long enough to test it. Every -tavān or -tavatī in one paragraph belongs to the same person, so a paragraph is masculine throughout or feminine throughout. The plural participial past is written nowhere in this course, so a past habit still belongs to one speaker.

WHAT THIS MODULE DOES NOT ADD. No new time word — L4-M6 owns pūrvam, paścāt, yadā, tadā and adhunā, and this module only spends them. No counterfactual, which is L4-M3's. No formal register, which is L4-M7's alone. No clock and no calendar, deferred since L2-M6. And no augmented verb of any kind beyond the one cell above.

sentences.cue: I used to go to school every day.

words.note: L4-M6's 'formerly'. In front of a participial past it is what turns one completed action into a habit.
L1-M1's 'I', and the gender the participle at the end agrees with.
L1-M4's 'daily'. It is the word that makes this a habit rather than one journey.
L1-M6's school, as the destination — the accusative marks it and no word for 'to' is written.
L1-M2's participial past, unchanged. A habitual past uses the ordinary one; nothing about the verb marks the habit.

sentences.trap: Nothing in the verb says 'used to'. Take pratidinam out and the same words mean 'I went to school', once. The habit is carried by the two adverbs alone.

variations.display: pūrvam aham pratidinam vidyālayam gatavatī.
variations.script: पूर्वम् अहम् प्रतिदिनम् विद्यालयम् गतवती।
variations.cue: I used to go to school every day.
variations.changed: a woman speaks; only the participle forks, and it forks once for the whole paragraph and not sentence by sentence

variations.display: pūrvam aham vidyālayam gatavān.
variations.script: पूर्वम् अहम् विद्यालयम् गतवान्।
variations.cue: I went to school.
variations.changed: pratidinam comes out and the habit goes with it — what is left is one completed journey

variations.display: adhunā api aham pratidinam vidyālayam gacchāmi.
variations.script: अधुना अपि अहम् प्रतिदिनम् विद्यालयम् गच्छामि।
variations.cue: I still go to school every day.
variations.changed: the past becomes the present and pūrvam becomes adhunā api; the frequency word is the only thing that stays put

sentences.usage: The ordinary opening of a story about how things used to be.

sentences.cue: As a child I studied Sanskrit every day.

words.note: 'In childhood' — the 'in' shape of bālyam, L1-M7's place case doing time. It points at a stretch of life and needs no date.
L1-M4's 'daily'.
L1-M1's Sanskrit, as the thing studied.
L1-M4's participial past. A woman says paṭhitavatī.

variations.display: bālye aham pratidinam saṃskṛtam paṭhitavatī.
variations.script: बाल्ये अहम् प्रतिदिनम् संस्कृतम् पठितवती।
variations.cue: As a child I studied Sanskrit every day.
variations.changed: a woman speaks; bālye does not move, because a place-shaped time word has no gender to agree with

variations.display: bālye aham saṃskṛtam na paṭhitavān.
variations.script: बाल्ये अहम् संस्कृतम् न पठितवान्।
variations.cue: As a child I did not study Sanskrit.
variations.changed: the habit is denied; na stands in front of the participle and pratidinam has nothing left to count

variations.display: bālye aham pratidinam saṃskṛtam paṭhitavān, adhunā api paṭhāmi.
variations.script: बाल्ये अहम् प्रतिदिनम् संस्कृतम् पठितवान्, अधुना अपि पठामि।
variations.cue: As a child I studied Sanskrit every day, and I still do.
variations.changed: a second half is added with adhunā api, which is how this course says 'still'

sentences.usage: Said of something that started long before the sentence does.

sentences.display: pūrvam mama gṛham hrasvam āsīt, adhunā mama gṛham navam asti.
sentences.script: पूर्वम् मम गृहम् ह्रस्वम् आसीत्, अधुना मम गृहम् नवम् अस्ति।
sentences.cue: My house used to be small; now my house is new.
sentences.literal: formerly my house small was, now my house new is

words.note: L4-M6's 'formerly'. In front of a participial past it is what turns one completed action into a habit.
L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape.
L1-M6's house in its naming shape — here what the sentence is about, not where anybody is.
L2-M3's adjective, neuter to agree with gṛham.
'Was', third singular and nothing else. It is the one imperfect this course writes, and it says how something STOOD — L2-M8's jātam is for what happened.
L4-M6's 'now'. It heads the second half of a then-and-now and answers pūrvam without being a ta- word.
L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape, repeated because the second half is a full clause of its own.
L1-M6's house, subject of the second half.
L2-M3's adjective, neuter to agree with gṛham.
L1-M3's present 'is'. Set beside āsīt it is what makes the two halves a then and a now.

sentences.trap: āsīt and asti are the same verb at two times, and this sentence is the clearest place to see it. Neither of them is a participle, and neither of them agrees with anybody's gender.
sentences.sound: POOR-vam MA-ma GRI-ham HRAS-vam AA-seet, a-dhu-NAA MA-ma GRI-ham NA-vam AS-ti.

variations.display: pūrvam mama gṛham hrasvam āsīt.
variations.script: पूर्वम् मम गृहम् ह्रस्वम् आसीत्।
variations.cue: My house used to be small.
variations.changed: the now half is dropped; āsīt alone is enough to put a state in the past

variations.display: kim bālye bhavān atra āsīt?
variations.script: किम् बाल्ये भवान् अत्र आसीत्?
variations.cue: Were you here as a child?
variations.changed: āsīt takes bhavān perfectly well, because bhavān has always taken a third-person verb — it is aham that it cannot take

variations.display: pūrvam mama gṛham hrasvam na āsīt.
variations.script: पूर्वम् मम गृहम् ह्रस्वम् न आसीत्।
variations.cue: My house did not used to be small.
variations.changed: the state is denied; na stands in front of āsīt exactly as it stands in front of asti

mistake.why: āsīt is third singular and has no person here to agree with aham. 'I was a student' is pūrvam aham chātraḥ, with no copula at all — which is how this course has said 'I am a student' since L1-M1, with pūrvam doing the rest.

sentences.usage: The plainest then-and-now sentence the course can build.

sentences.display: bālye mama abhyāsaḥ uttamaḥ āsīt, adhunā abhyāsaḥ na asti.
sentences.script: बाल्ये मम अभ्यासः उत्तमः आसीत्, अधुना अभ्यासः न अस्ति।
sentences.cue: In childhood my practice was excellent; now there is no practice.
sentences.literal: in-childhood my practice excellent was, now practice not is

words.note: 'In childhood' — the 'in' shape of bālyam, L1-M7's place case doing time. It points at a stretch of life and needs no date.
L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape.
'A regular habit', masculine. It names the habit rather than describing it: mama abhyāsaḥ uttamaḥ āsīt.
L2-M3's adjective, masculine to agree with abhyāsaḥ.
'Was', third singular and nothing else. It is the one imperfect this course writes, and it says how something STOOD — L2-M8's jātam is for what happened.
L4-M6's 'now'. It heads the second half of a then-and-now and answers pūrvam without being a ta- word.
The same word again, this time the subject of the present half.
L1-M2's 'not', in front of asti.
L1-M3's present 'is'.

variations.display: bālye mama abhyāsaḥ uttamaḥ āsīt.
variations.script: बाल्ये मम अभ्यासः उत्तमः आसीत्।
variations.cue: In childhood my practice was excellent.
variations.changed: the now half is dropped and the sentence is a plain statement about a state that has passed

variations.display: bālye mama abhyāsaḥ na āsīt, adhunā asti.
variations.script: बाल्ये मम अभ्यासः न आसीत्, अधुना अस्ति।
variations.cue: In childhood I had no practice; now I do.
variations.changed: the two halves trade signs, which reverses the whole story without moving a word

variations.display: adhunā api mama abhyāsaḥ uttamaḥ asti.
variations.script: अधुना अपि मम अभ्यासः उत्तमः अस्ति।
variations.cue: My practice is still excellent.
variations.changed: the then half is dropped and adhunā takes api behind it, which is L4-M6's 'still'

sentences.usage: Said of a discipline you have let go of, or kept.

sentences.display: pūrvam aham pratidinam dugdham pītavān, adhunā jalam pibāmi.
sentences.script: पूर्वम् अहम् प्रतिदिनम् दुग्धम् पीतवान्, अधुना जलम् पिबामि।
sentences.cue: I used to drink milk every day; now I drink water.
sentences.literal: formerly I every-day milk drank, now water I-drink

words.note: L4-M6's 'formerly'. In front of a participial past it is what turns one completed action into a habit.
L1-M1's 'I'. It appears once and covers both halves, because the -mi of the second already says who.
L1-M4's 'daily', the word that makes the first half a habit.
L2-M5's milk, as the thing drunk.
L1-M4's participial past. A woman says pītavatī.
L4-M6's 'now'. It heads the second half of a then-and-now and answers pūrvam without being a ta- word.
L1-M3's water, as the thing drunk now.
L1-M4's drinking verb in the first singular.

sentences.sound: POOR-vam a-HAM pra-ti-DI-nam DUG-dham pee-ta-VAAN, a-dhu-NAA JA-lam pi-BAA-mi.

variations.display: pūrvam aham pratidinam dugdham pītavatī, adhunā jalam pibāmi.
variations.script: पूर्वम् अहम् प्रतिदिनम् दुग्धम् पीतवती, अधुना जलम् पिबामि।
variations.cue: I used to drink milk every day; now I drink water.
variations.changed: a woman speaks, so the participle forks and the present does not — a present tense marks person and never gender

variations.display: pūrvam aham pratidinam dugdham pītavān, adhunā api pibāmi.
variations.script: पूर्वम् अहम् प्रतिदिनम् दुग्धम् पीतवान्, अधुना अपि पिबामि।
variations.cue: I used to drink milk every day, and I still do.
variations.changed: the second half becomes a continuation with adhunā api, and the thing drunk is understood rather than repeated

variations.display: adhunā aham pratidinam jalam pibāmi.
variations.script: अधुना अहम् प्रतिदिनम् जलम् पिबामि।
variations.cue: Now I drink water every day.
variations.changed: the then half is dropped altogether and the frequency word moves to the half that keeps it

mistake.display: pūrvam aham pratidinam dugdham pītavatī, adhunā jalam pibāmi, pūrvam phalam khāditavān.
mistake.why: The participle changes gender halfway through. A paragraph of participial pasts belongs to ONE speaker, so it is pītavatī and khāditavatī together, or pītavān and khāditavān together — never one of each.

sentences.usage: How a change of habit is actually reported.

sentences.display: adhunā api aham pratidinam saṃskṛtam paṭhāmi.
sentences.script: अधुना अपि अहम् प्रतिदिनम् संस्कृतम् पठामि।
sentences.cue: I still study Sanskrit every day.
sentences.literal: now even I every-day Sanskrit read

words.note: L4-M6's 'now'. It heads the second half of a then-and-now and answers pūrvam without being a ta- word.
L1-M10's api behind adhunā. The two together are L4-M6's 'still', and they stay two words.
L1-M4's 'daily'. In a present sentence it makes an ongoing habit, exactly as it makes a past one.
L1-M1's Sanskrit.
L1-M4's reading verb in the first singular.

variations.display: adhunā api aham pratidinam saṃskṛtam na paṭhāmi.
variations.script: अधुना अपि अहम् प्रतिदिनम् संस्कृतम् न पठामि।
variations.cue: I still do not study Sanskrit every day.
variations.changed: the verb is negated and 'still' survives in front of it, leaning on the whole clause

variations.display: pūrvam aham pratidinam saṃskṛtam paṭhitavān.
variations.script: पूर्वम् अहम् प्रतिदिनम् संस्कृतम् पठितवान्।
variations.cue: I used to study Sanskrit every day.
variations.changed: the same habit in the past: only the time word and the verb move, and pratidinam does not

variations.display: bālye aham saṃskṛtam paṭhitavān, adhunā api paṭhāmi.
variations.script: बाल्ये अहम् संस्कृतम् पठितवान्, अधुना अपि पठामि।
variations.cue: I studied Sanskrit as a child, and I still do.
variations.changed: both halves in one sentence, which is the shape this whole module is built out of

sentences.usage: The other half of every then-and-now: what did not change.

sentences.display: bālye mama gṛhe ekaḥ dīpaḥ āsīt.
sentences.script: बाल्ये मम गृहे एकः दीपः आसीत्।
sentences.cue: In childhood there was one lamp in my house.
sentences.literal: in-childhood my in-house one lamp was

words.note: 'In childhood' — the 'in' shape of bālyam, L1-M7's place case doing time. It points at a stretch of life and needs no date.
L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape.
L1-M6's house in its 'in' shape.
L1-M8's numeral, masculine to agree with dīpaḥ.
L3-M9's lamp in its naming shape, the thing whose being there is stated.
'Was', third singular and nothing else. It is the one imperfect this course writes, and it says how something STOOD — L2-M8's jātam is for what happened.

sentences.trap: āsīt here is 'there was', not 'was something'. The same word covers both, exactly as L1-M3's asti covers 'is' and 'there is'.
sentences.sound: BAAL-yeh MA-ma GRI-heh EH-kah DEE-pah AA-seet.

variations.display: bālye mama gṛhe dīpaḥ na āsīt.
variations.script: बाल्ये मम गृहे दीपः न आसीत्।
variations.cue: In childhood there was no lamp in my house.
variations.changed: the numeral comes out and the existence is denied — na in front of āsīt as in front of asti

variations.display: adhunā mama gṛhe ekaḥ dīpaḥ asti.
variations.script: अधुना मम गृहे एकः दीपः अस्ति।
variations.cue: Now there is one lamp in my house.
variations.changed: the same statement in the present, which is the only word that had to change

variations.display: bālye mama gṛhe ekaḥ dīpaḥ āsīt, adhunā daśa santi.
variations.script: बाल्ये मम गृहे एकः दीपः आसीत्, अधुना दश सन्ति।
variations.cue: In childhood there was one lamp in my house; now there are ten.
variations.changed: the now half takes L3-M9's plural santi, because āsīt has no plural in this course and the present does

sentences.usage: The kind of detail a childhood story is made of.

sentences.display: pūrvam atra vidyālayaḥ āsīt, adhunā atra kāryālayaḥ asti.
sentences.script: पूर्वम् अत्र विद्यालयः आसीत्, अधुना अत्र कार्यालयः अस्ति।
sentences.cue: There used to be a school here; now there is an office here.
sentences.literal: formerly here school was, now here office is

words.note: L4-M6's 'formerly'. In front of a participial past it is what turns one completed action into a habit.
L1-M7's 'here', opening both halves.
L1-M6's school in its naming shape — what stood here, not where anybody went.
'Was', third singular and nothing else. It is the one imperfect this course writes, and it says how something STOOD — L2-M8's jātam is for what happened.
L4-M6's 'now'. It heads the second half of a then-and-now and answers pūrvam without being a ta- word.
L1-M7's 'here' again, because the second half is a full clause.
L3-M8's office in its naming shape.
L1-M3's present 'is'.

sentences.sound: POOR-vam A-tra vid-YAA-la-yah AA-seet, a-dhu-NAA A-tra KAAR-yaa-la-yah AS-ti.

variations.display: pūrvam atra vidyālayaḥ āsīt.
variations.script: पूर्वम् अत्र विद्यालयः आसीत्।
variations.cue: There used to be a school here.
variations.changed: the now half is dropped and the sentence says only what has gone

variations.display: pūrvam atra vidyālayaḥ na āsīt, adhunā atra vidyālayaḥ asti.
variations.script: पूर्वम् अत्र विद्यालयः न आसीत्, अधुना अत्र विद्यालयः अस्ति।
variations.cue: There was no school here before; now there is one.
variations.changed: the signs are reversed, which turns a loss into an arrival

variations.display: yadā aham bālaḥ tadā atra vidyālayaḥ āsīt.
variations.script: यदा अहम् बालः तदा अत्र विद्यालयः आसीत्।
variations.cue: When I was a boy there was a school here.
variations.changed: L4-M6's yadā … tadā carries the time instead of pūrvam, and the ya- clause has no verb at all — aham bālaḥ needs none

mistake.why: This asks how things STOOD yesterday, which is rarely the question meant. 'What happened yesterday?' is L2-M8's hyaḥ kim jātam — āsīt is the state and jātam is the event.

sentences.usage: Said in front of a building that is not what it was.

sentences.display: bālye aham pratidinam mandiram gatavān, adhunā tatra na gacchāmi.
sentences.script: बाल्ये अहम् प्रतिदिनम् मन्दिरम् गतवान्, अधुना तत्र न गच्छामि।
sentences.cue: As a child I went to the temple every day; now I do not go there.
sentences.literal: in-childhood I every-day temple went, now there not I-go

words.note: 'In childhood' — the 'in' shape of bālyam, L1-M7's place case doing time. It points at a stretch of life and needs no date.
L1-M1's 'I', once for the whole sentence.
L1-M4's 'daily'.
L3-M9's temple, as the destination.
L1-M2's participial past. A woman says gatavatī.
L4-M6's 'now'. It heads the second half of a then-and-now and answers pūrvam without being a ta- word.
L1-M7's 'there', standing in for the destination so it need not be named twice.
L1-M2's 'not', in front of the present verb.
L1-M2's going verb in the first singular.

variations.display: bālye aham pratidinam mandiram gatavatī, adhunā tatra na gacchāmi.
variations.script: बाल्ये अहम् प्रतिदिनम् मन्दिरम् गतवती, अधुना तत्र न गच्छामि।
variations.cue: As a child I went to the temple every day; now I do not go there.
variations.changed: a woman speaks and the one participle forks; nothing in the present half moves

variations.display: bālye aham pratidinam mandiram gatavān, adhunā api tatra gacchāmi.
variations.script: बाल्ये अहम् प्रतिदिनम् मन्दिरम् गतवान्, अधुना अपि तत्र गच्छामि।
variations.cue: As a child I went to the temple every day, and I still go there.
variations.changed: the second half flips from a stop to a continuation, with na replaced by api behind adhunā

variations.display: bālye aham mandiram gatvā paścāt gṛhe paṭhitavān.
variations.script: बाल्ये अहम् मन्दिरम् गत्वा पश्चात् गृहे पठितवान्।
variations.cue: As a child I went to the temple and then studied at home.
variations.changed: L3-M1's absolutive and L4-M6's paścāt put two childhood actions in order inside one sentence

sentences.usage: A habit named and then dropped, which is the module's whole shape.

sentences.display: bālye mama bhrātā śāntaḥ āsīt, adhunā saḥ kruddhaḥ asti.
sentences.script: बाल्ये मम भ्राता शान्तः आसीत्, अधुना सः क्रुद्धः अस्ति।
sentences.cue: In childhood my brother was calm; now he is angry.
sentences.literal: in-childhood my brother calm was, now he angry is

words.note: 'In childhood' — the 'in' shape of bālyam, L1-M7's place case doing time. It points at a stretch of life and needs no date.
L1-M1's aham in its 'of me' shape.
L2-M2's brother in his naming shape.
L2-M2's adjective, masculine to agree with bhrātā. A woman is śāntā.
'Was', third singular and nothing else. It is the one imperfect this course writes, and it says how something STOOD — L2-M8's jātam is for what happened.
L4-M6's 'now'. It heads the second half of a then-and-now and answers pūrvam without being a ta- word.
L1-M5's 'he', standing in for the brother so the second half need not name him again.
L3-M6's adjective, masculine to agree with saḥ.
L1-M3's present 'is'.

sentences.trap: āsīt does not agree with bhrātā in gender, and asti does not agree with saḥ. Only the adjectives do — a Sanskrit verb marks person and number and never gender.
sentences.sound: BAAL-yeh MA-ma BHRAA-taa SHAAN-tah AA-seet, a-dhu-NAA sah KRUD-dhah AS-ti.

variations.display: bālye mama bhaginī śāntā āsīt, adhunā sā kruddhā asti.
variations.script: बाल्ये मम भगिनी शान्ता आसीत्, अधुना सा क्रुद्धा अस्ति।
variations.cue: In childhood my sister was calm; now she is angry.
variations.changed: the person becomes a woman: both adjectives and the pronoun fork, and neither verb moves

variations.display: bālye mama bhrātā śāntaḥ āsīt, adhunā api śāntaḥ asti.
variations.script: बाल्ये मम भ्राता शान्तः आसीत्, अधुना अपि शान्तः अस्ति।
variations.cue: In childhood my brother was calm, and he is still calm.
variations.changed: the second half becomes a continuation instead of a contrast, which is what adhunā api always does

variations.display: kim bālye bhavataḥ bhrātā śāntaḥ āsīt?
variations.script: किम् बाल्ये भवतः भ्राता शान्तः आसीत्?
variations.cue: Was your brother calm as a child?
variations.changed: L1-M2's kim makes a question and the brother becomes the listener's, with L1-M2's polite 'your'

sentences.usage: The everyday then-and-now about somebody else.
sentences.mnemonic: The adjectives fork; the verbs do not.

comprehensionPool.cue: As a child I drank milk every day.

comprehensionPool.display: pūrvam mama mitram atra āsīt, adhunā tatra asti.
comprehensionPool.script: पूर्वम् मम मित्रम् अत्र आसीत्, अधुना तत्र अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: My friend used to be here; now he is there.

comprehensionPool.display: pūrvam atra mārgaḥ hrasvaḥ āsīt, adhunā dīrghaḥ asti.
comprehensionPool.script: पूर्वम् अत्र मार्गः ह्रस्वः आसीत्, अधुना दीर्घः अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: The road here used to be short; now it is long.
In childhood my practice was excellent.

comprehensionPool.display: adhunā api mama pitā kāryālayam gacchati.
comprehensionPool.script: अधुना अपि मम पिता कार्यालयम् गच्छति।
comprehensionPool.cue: My father still goes to the office.
My sister used to write every day.

comprehensionPool.display: bālye atra pustakālayaḥ āsīt, adhunā atra vidyālayaḥ asti.
comprehensionPool.script: बाल्ये अत्र पुस्तकालयः आसीत्, अधुना अत्र विद्यालयः अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: There used to be a library here; now there is a school.

comprehensionPool.display: pūrvam aham kāryālayam gatavān, adhunā gṛhe kāryam karomi.
comprehensionPool.script: पूर्वम् अहम् कार्यालयम् गतवान्, अधुना गृहे कार्यम् करोमि।
comprehensionPool.cue: I used to go to the office; now I do the work at home.

comprehensionPool.display: bālye mama abhyāsaḥ na āsīt, adhunā asti.
comprehensionPool.script: बाल्ये मम अभ्यासः न आसीत्, अधुना अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: In childhood I had no practice; now I do.

comprehensionPool.display: adhunā api aham pratidinam jalam pibāmi.
comprehensionPool.script: अधुना अपि अहम् प्रतिदिनम् जलम् पिबामि।
comprehensionPool.cue: I still drink water every day.

comprehensionPool.display: bālye aham vidyālayam gatvā paścāt gṛhe paṭhitavān.
comprehensionPool.script: बाल्ये अहम् विद्यालयम् गत्वा पश्चात् गृहे पठितवान्।
comprehensionPool.cue: As a child I went to school and then studied at home.

comprehensionPool.display: pūrvam atra mandiram āsīt, adhunā atra gṛham asti.
comprehensionPool.script: पूर्वम् अत्र मन्दिरम् आसीत्, अधुना अत्र गृहम् अस्ति।
comprehensionPool.cue: There used to be a temple here; now there is a house.
My mother studied Sanskrit in her childhood.
